stem: A disposable dressing is saturated with blood and would release blood in a liquid or semiliquid state if compressed. How should the item be classified under the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard?

options.A: As contaminated sharps waste because any item containing visible blood requires a puncture-resistant sharps container.
options.B: As pharmaceutical waste because blood-contaminated materials are disposed through the medication-waste stream.
options.C: As regulated waste because it would release blood in a liquid or semiliquid state if compressed.
options.D: As ordinary solid waste because disposable dressings are excluded from regulated waste regardless of saturation.

rationale: OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard defines regulated waste to include contaminated items that would release blood or other potentially infectious materials in a liquid or semiliquid state if compressed. The dressing in the stem meets that explicit regulatory criterion, so C is correct. It is not a contaminated sharp merely because blood is present, it is not pharmaceutical waste, and saturation sufficient to release blood means it cannot be treated as ordinary solid waste under this definition.
educational_objective: Classify blood-contaminated disposable material as OSHA regulated waste when compression would release blood or other potentially infectious material in a liquid or semiliquid state.
source_locator: 29 CFR 1910.1030(b) Definitions > Regulated Waste: includes contaminated items that would release blood or OPIM in a liquid or semiliquid state if compressed. 1910.1030(d)(4)(iii) specifies containment/disposal requirements for regulated waste.
source_claim_supported: A blood-saturated dressing that would release liquid or semiliquid blood when compressed meets OSHA's definition of regulated waste.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: apply bloodborne-pathogen precautions, handle contaminated materials safely, and follow regulatory infection-control practices.
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — blood-contaminated regulated waste classification

options.B: Classify it as pharmaceutical waste because blood-contaminated material is disposed through the medication-waste stream.

source_original.rationale: OSHA defines regulated waste to include contaminated items that would release blood or other potentially infectious material in a liquid or semiliquid state if compressed. The stem was narrowed from the vague phrase 'blood-soaked' to the regulatory criterion that determines classification.

audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item mirrors the legal/regulatory definition directly and does not infer regulated-waste status merely from visible blood volume.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because only contaminated sharps require sharps-container classification; a dressing is not a sharp.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because blood-contaminated dressings are not pharmaceutical waste.
distractor_audit.C: Correct and directly supported by OSHA's definition.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because items that release liquid/semiliquid blood when compressed are explicitly regulated waste.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only C matches the exact regulatory criterion stated in the stem.
